rules.explanation: Hypersensitivity to capecitabine, oxaliplatin or an excipient is an exclusion.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding are protocol exclusions.

Known complete DPD deficiency is a contraindication to capecitabine.

action.recommendation: Consider an individualised reduced capecitabine starting dose with careful monitoring.

action.recommendation: Confirm DPD testing before first capecitabine treatment unless previously tested.

Baseline ANC below 1.5 or platelets below 100 should not be treated with capecitabine.
If ANC remains below 1.2 or platelets below 75 after two weeks, discontinue treatment.
Hold treatment and repeat FBC weekly when ANC is below 1.2 or platelets below 75 on day 1.
After recovery, a grade 3 delayed-week nadir requires both drugs to be reduced by one dose level.
After recovery, a grade 4 delayed-week nadir requires both drugs to be reduced by two dose levels.

action.recommendation: Use 75% of the original capecitabine dose.

rules.explanation: CrCl 30–50 mL/min requires capecitabine at 75% of the original dose.

action.recommendation: Capecitabine is not recommended; consider oxaliplatin at 50% only after Consultant review.

rules.explanation: For CrCl below 30 mL/min capecitabine is not recommended and oxaliplatin may be considered at 50%.

action.recommendation: Capecitabine is not recommended; consider oxaliplatin at 50% with haemodialysis within 90 minutes after administration.

rules.explanation: For haemodialysis, capecitabine is not recommended; oxaliplatin may be considered at 50% with dialysis timing specified.

action.until: bilirubin is 3 ×ULN or less and ALT/AST are 2.5 ×ULN or less

rules.explanation: Withhold capecitabine for bilirubin above 3 ×ULN or ALT/AST above 2.5 ×ULN.
If diarrhoea remains grade 2 or greater after two weeks, discontinue treatment.
Grade 2 or greater diarrhoea on day 1 requires treatment to be held and reviewed weekly.
After recovery from grade 3 diarrhoea, reduce capecitabine by one dose level.
After recovery from grade 4 diarrhoea, reduce oxaliplatin by one dose level and capecitabine by two dose levels.
If stomatitis remains grade 2 or greater after two weeks, discontinue treatment.
Grade 2 or greater stomatitis on day 1 requires treatment to be held and reviewed weekly.
After recovery from grade 3 stomatitis, reduce capecitabine by one dose level.
After recovery from grade 4 stomatitis, reduce oxaliplatin by one dose level and capecitabine by two dose levels.
If hand-foot syndrome remains grade 2 or greater after two weeks, discontinue treatment.
Grade 2 or greater hand-foot syndrome on day 1 requires treatment to be held and reviewed weekly.
After recovery from grade 3 hand-foot syndrome, reduce capecitabine by one dose level.
Grade 2 paraesthesia persisting until the next cycle requires oxaliplatin 100 mg/m².
Grade 3 paraesthesia lasting more than seven days but resolving before the next cycle requires oxaliplatin 100 mg/m².
Grade 3 paraesthesia persisting until the next cycle requires oxaliplatin discontinuation.
Grade 4 neuropathy of any duration requires oxaliplatin discontinuation.

action.recommendation: Increase oxaliplatin infusion duration to 4–6 hours.

rules.explanation: Increase oxaliplatin infusion time to 4–6 hours after laryngopharyngeal dysaesthesia.

patient.title: CAPOX / XELOX

agents.name: Capecitabine
agents.explanation: The body converts capecitabine into fluorouracil, which disrupts DNA and RNA processes needed for cell growth. Tablets are active chemotherapy; taking them at home still requires a clear monitoring and interruption plan.
agents.watch: Stop tablets and contact the team for significant diarrhoea, painful mouth ulcers, hand-foot soreness affecting activities, fever or dehydration. Chest pain needs urgent assessment. Do not restart until instructed.
risks: Severe early toxicity including DPD-related toxicity

agents.name: Oxaliplatin
agents.explanation: Oxaliplatin makes links within DNA. These interfere with copying and repair, which can stop a cancer cell dividing. Healthy tissues can also be affected.
agents.watch: Cold can trigger tingling or throat discomfort. Tell the team about persistent numbness, difficulty with buttons or walking, or infusion symptoms. New breathing difficulty always needs assessment.
risks: Persistent sensory neuropathy, sometimes lasting after treatment
Rare serious lung or blood complications

HSE: chemotherapy side effects and urgent advice

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide if blood results are safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions require the clinical protocol, symptoms, previous toxicity, organ function and the prescriber’s review. The patient page explains the checks and does not authorise treatment.

patient.phases_note: The treating team confirms the indication, schedule and duration. Changes are recorded on your own prescription.
patient.medicines_title: Your medicines and what they do
patient.timeline_note: Bars show planned treatment and possible symptom patterns, not measured risk. Side effects can overlap and persist.
patient.safety_note: There are no guaranteed safe days. Act on fever, sudden illness or a new serious symptom whenever it occurs. Do not wait for the next appointment.
patient.teachback: Can you explain which medicines you are receiving, the schedule, the contact plan and the symptoms that need prompt help?
patient.consent_support: Confirm DPD testing, renal review, the exact tablet prescription, missed-dose and interruption instructions, cold precautions and anti-sickness plan.
patient.urgent_extra: New chest pain, breathing difficulty, severe diarrhoea, inability to drink, reduced urine, uncontrolled bleeding or a rapidly worsening symptom needs prompt assessment.

chapters.title: Treatment aim and duration
chapters.intro: CAPOX is used in several distinct settings.

items.title: Adjuvant colon cancer
items.text: Following resection of stage III colon cancer, CAPOX aims to reduce recurrence risk. Duration is a discussion about cancer risk and toxicity; three and six months are not interchangeable for everyone.

items.title: Advanced colorectal cancer
items.text: The aim may be cancer control, symptom relief and longer survival. Molecular findings, previous therapy and fitness affect the overall plan. Additional targeted medicines require their own regimen and counselling.

items.title: After gastric surgery
items.text: The adjuvant gastric evidence concerns a specific postoperative setting after D2 gastrectomy. Nutrition, postoperative recovery and oral tolerance need particular attention.

items.title: Alternatives and review points
items.text: Ask why this oral/infusion combination was chosen, whether an infusional alternative is suitable, and what would prompt a pause or change. Taking tablets at home does not mean the treatment is mild.

chapters.title: Taking capecitabine safely
chapters.intro: Your prescription is the authority for dose and dates.

items.title: Food, doses and tablet handling
items.text: Take doses about 12 hours apart and within 30 minutes after food, as instructed. Swallow whole with water. If swallowing is difficult, ask the oncology pharmacist for a safe plan. Do not crush tablets or improvise a liquid.

items.title: Missed or vomited doses
items.text: Do not replace a missed or vomited dose and do not take an extra dose. Record it and resume the next scheduled dose only if otherwise safe under your written instructions. Repeated vomiting or uncertainty needs a call.

items.title: When to stop and call
items.text: Do not continue through significant diarrhoea, painful mouth sores, painful hand-foot symptoms, fever, dehydration or chest pain. Stop capecitabine and obtain prompt advice. A clinician decides whether and how to restart.

items.title: The rest week is part of treatment
items.text: Days without tablets are planned. Do not fill them with leftovers. Return unused medicine through the hospital/pharmacy process and keep it out of household waste and away from other people.

chapters.title: What the checks are for
chapters.intro: Symptoms, blood results and the treatment aim answer different questions.

items.title: Blood counts
items.text: Neutrophils protect against infection, haemoglobin carries oxygen and platelets help clotting. A normal previous result or feeling well does not prove the current counts are safe. Fever or sudden illness needs immediate advice.

items.title: Kidney and liver function
items.text: Organ function can change drug exposure. Vomiting or diarrhoea can cause dehydration and worsen kidney function. Report reduced urine, poor intake, jaundice and new medicines. The clinical assessment combines results with symptoms.

items.title: Describe symptoms in practical terms
items.text: Tell the team about the worst symptoms since the last visit, even if improved today. Examples include extra stools above your usual pattern, whether mouth pain affects drinking, and whether numbness affects buttons or balance.

items.title: How benefit is assessed
items.text: After surgery, treatment aims to reduce the chance of recurrence; there may be no visible cancer to measure. In advanced disease, scans, symptoms and function help assess control. Ask when review is planned and what would lead to a change.

chapters.title: Separate the symptoms from the cause
chapters.intro: You do not need to diagnose an adverse effect before calling.

items.title: Hand-foot syndrome versus neuropathy
items.text: Capecitabine can cause tender, red or peeling palms and soles. Oxaliplatin more often causes cold-triggered tingling and cumulative numbness. Both can affect walking or hand use. Tell the team about both the sensation and what you can no longer do.

items.title: Diarrhoea and dehydration
items.text: Record stools above your own usual pattern, night-time symptoms and stoma output if relevant. Reduced urine, dizziness, inability to drink or worsening diarrhoea needs prompt advice. A medicine to stop diarrhoea does not replace the interruption plan.

items.title: Mouth, appetite and fatigue
items.text: Mouth soreness can make food and fluid difficult. Start gentle mouth care and report painful swallowing or reduced intake. Ask for symptom and nutritional support. New major weakness or breathlessness needs assessment.

items.title: Heart or infusion symptoms
items.text: Fluoropyrimidines can cause serious cardiac effects; oxaliplatin can cause allergic reactions. New chest symptoms, fainting or breathing difficulty need urgent assessment. Do not assume these are anxiety or ordinary cold sensitivity.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: Plan around the activities and people that matter to you.

items.title: Food, drink and practical help
items.text: Use foods and drinks you can manage. Tell the team about weight loss, poor intake or difficulty shopping and cooking; ask for dietitian or practical support. A fixed daily fluid target is not appropriate for everyone, particularly with heart or kidney problems.

items.title: Activity, rest and driving
items.text: Balance rest with manageable activity. Record what fatigue stops you doing. Do not drive when dizzy, unwell or affected by sedating medicines. Ask about work adjustments and transport for treatment days.

items.title: Medicines, vaccines and supplements
items.text: Bring a complete medicine list, including over-the-counter products and supplements. Ask the oncology pharmacist before changes. Discuss vaccination timing. Do not stop prescribed long-term medicines on your own.

items.title: Fertility, contraception and breastfeeding
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation before treatment when relevant. Ask for a written contraception and breastfeeding plan covering each medicine and the period after treatment. Tell the team promptly about a possible pregnancy.

items.title: Support for you and your family
items.text: Ask about psycho-oncology, social work, counselling and symptom support. Take information in manageable amounts. A family member or trusted person can help record questions if you wish. Discuss how treatment fits your priorities.

chapters.title: The names on your treatment plan
chapters.intro: Useful terms for clinic and pharmacy.

items.title: CAPOX, XELOX and fluoropyrimidine
items.text: CAPOX and XELOX name the same capecitabine–oxaliplatin combination. Capecitabine is a fluoropyrimidine, a drug family that includes fluorouracil. It is not interchangeable dose-for-dose with another tablet or infusion.

items.title: Adherence and interruption
items.text: Adherence means following the agreed plan, including stopping for toxicity when instructed. Interrupting tablets and calling about a serious symptom is part of safe treatment, not a failure to comply.

patient.purpose: CAPOX, also called XELOX, combines capecitabine tablets with oxaliplatin infusion. This NCCP protocol covers adjuvant stage III colon cancer, advanced colorectal cancer and adjuvant gastric cancer after D2 surgery. Confirm the treatment aim and duration for your indication.
patient.schedule_summary: Oxaliplatin on Day 1; capecitabine twice daily on Days 1–14, followed by Days 15–21 without capecitabine. Follow your individual prescription.

phases.label: 21-day treatment cycle
phases.detail: Oxaliplatin on Day 1; capecitabine twice daily on Days 1–14, followed by Days 15–21 without capecitabine. Follow your individual prescription.

timeline.label: Hands / feet / bowel
timeline.text: May accumulate; continue watching in rest week

timeline.label: Blood counts / infection
timeline.text: Act on symptoms on any day

day_groups.title: Infusion and tablet plan
day_groups.body: Your team checks symptoms, blood results and the oral prescription. Make sure you know the tablet strengths, number per dose and exact start and stop instructions.
day_groups.action: Use the written prescription. Take capecitabine with water within 30 minutes after food; never guess the tablet count.

day_groups.title: Tablets at home
day_groups.body: Continue twice-daily capecitabine according to the prescription. A missed or vomited dose is not replaced. Record doses missed and contact the team if you are unsure.
day_groups.action: Do not double the next dose. Keep tablets in the original packaging, away from children; do not crush or split unless the oncology pharmacist has arranged it.

day_groups.title: Watch for accumulating symptoms
day_groups.body: Diarrhoea, mouth ulcers or painful hands and feet can develop or worsen. Poor intake and dehydration can worsen kidney function and increase risk from capecitabine.
day_groups.action: Stop tablets and contact oncology for significant diarrhoea, painful mouth or hand-foot symptoms affecting activity, fever, dehydration or chest symptoms. Do not restart without advice.

day_groups.title: The prescribed tablet-free week
day_groups.body: No capecitabine is planned in this interval, but side effects and infection can still occur. Keep recording symptoms and confirm blood-test and review arrangements.
day_groups.action: Do not use leftover tablets to make up missed doses or start the next cycle early. The next cycle requires team confirmation.

support.title: Nausea prevention and rescue
support.text: Take the prescribed prevention medicines at the planned times and keep rescue treatment available. Tell the team if nausea or constipation is not controlled; do not duplicate steroid or anti-sickness medicines.

support.title: Bowel symptoms
support.text: Report diarrhoea promptly and follow the written rescue plan. Severe symptoms, fever, dehydration or inability to drink need urgent advice.

support.title: Counts and recovery
support.text: White-cell growth-factor injections are prescribed according to individual risk and previous complications. They are not automatically required for every patient or every cycle.

support.title: Cold and nerve symptoms
support.text: Avoid cold exposure as advised after oxaliplatin. Report persistent numbness or difficulty with buttons, walking or everyday tasks before the next dose.

support.title: Skin and mouth care
support.text: Use gentle skin and mouth care. Painful hands and feet or mouth sores can require a tablet hold and team review; do not continue simply to finish the pack.

evidence.title: Understanding the evidence
evidence.intro: Ask which evidence matches your cancer, treatment aim and medicines.
evidence.interpretation: A study of stage III colon cancer after surgery found better long-term outcomes with CAPOX than with the intravenous fluorouracil schedule studied. The duration decision and evidence for metastatic colorectal or postoperative gastric cancer need separate discussion.

chronology_notes.title: Treatment and rest
chronology_notes.text: The prescribed capecitabine course is followed by a tablet-free interval. Follow your own written start and stop instructions.

chronology_notes.title: Hands, feet and bowel
chronology_notes.text: Symptoms may accumulate during the tablet course and can continue into the rest week. Follow your stop-and-call instructions.

chronology_notes.title: Blood counts
chronology_notes.text: Infection can occur on any day, including the tablet-free week. Fever or sudden illness needs prompt contact.

chronology_notes.title: Cold and nerve symptoms
chronology_notes.text: Oxaliplatin can cause cold-triggered symptoms, and numbness may accumulate over cycles. Report functional changes before the next treatment.

patient.administration_text: Oxaliplatin is infused intravenously in glucose 5%; sodium chloride is incompatible. Capecitabine is taken orally with food on days 1–14.

sections.title: Before the first treatment
sections.text: Confirm the aim, likely course length, blood-test arrangements and a working urgent contact number. DPD testing is required before starting the fluoropyrimidine unless already completed.

sections.title: Taking the tablets
sections.text: Use the prescribed morning and evening dose within 30 minutes after food on the agreed treatment days. Do not make up a missed or vomited dose. Follow the team’s hold instructions for significant diarrhoea, mouth soreness or painful hands and feet, and contact them promptly.

sections.title: If treatment is delayed
sections.text: Ask the unit to confirm the new treatment and blood-test dates. Re-anchor supportive medicines to the treatment actually given; do not take an extra or catch-up anticancer dose yourself.

sections.title: Getting help between visits
sections.text: Follow your oncology unit’s urgent advice for fever, infection, severe diarrhoea, chest pain or difficulty breathing. Bring your treatment card and current medicines list.
